prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, which brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level of precision

statement.case_for: I moved the optical lattice clock from third place in my opening ballot to first. It is the entry where the committee can say most plainly what was discovered, who did it and why it matters. Katori's magic-wavelength idea removes the light shift that would otherwise ruin a trapped-atom clock. Ye's strontium clocks then took it to roughly 1e-18, and later to many-body effects in the lattice. That is a clean two-person credit with no collaboration problem. The measurements are independently reproduced in many national laboratories, and clock comparisons already test gravitational redshift over millimetres and the constancy of constants. This is exactly the kind of clue from nature that I say physics needs, rather than elegant theory waiting for confirmation. The redefinition of the second makes the timing good. My opening argument for IceCube still stands as a statement about a new window on the universe, but when I compare the two on attribution and on how settled the claim is, the clock is the stronger prize today.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is increment. Hall and Hansch (2005) and Wineland (2012) already honoured frequency combs and ion-based clocks and precision control, so a clock prize could look like a third award for the same neighbourhood of metrology. A second objection is that the lattice clock is an instrument and a technique, and its most fundamental physics (variation of constants, a gravitational-wave or dark-matter signal) has not yet been delivered. If the committee puts the discovery first, it may prefer a result that has already told us something new about the cosmos. Finally, Ye's credit also overlaps with the comb and cavity-stabilisation work that the 2005 prize touched, so the committee would need to word the citation so that it clearly rests on the lattice clock itself.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as a measurement technique that changed what can be measured, with a clean Katori and Ye credit and reproduction at JILA, RIKEN, PTB, NIST and SYRTE.
responses.response: I agree on the credit and the maturity, and this has moved me from my opening position. I would add a qualification to the 'changed what can be measured' argument. The strongest version of the case is not precision as such but what the precision has already shown, namely redshift tests at millimetre scale and the many-body clock physics. I would want the citation to say that, so that it does not read as a third award for better clocks after 2005 and 2012. On atom interferometry (B032), which Kroll ranks second, I am less convinced. The three-name credit is much harder to defend, and the precision claims, for example for G, are still contested.

responses.point: Pearce ranks aberration-corrected electron microscopy first and the Higgs experiments second, valuing enabling instruments, and accepts that the Higgs credit is hard to assign among thousands.
responses.response: I respect the instrument argument and I accept that aberration correction is a real, mature breakthrough. My reservation is about physics content for the Physics prize: sub-angstrom imaging is a tool whose physics results are mostly in materials science, and I do not find that it answers a question about nature in the way a clock or a neutrino telescope does. On the Higgs, I agree with Pearce that the science is beyond doubt but disagree that it is a practical option. Naming three people out of two collaborations of several thousand would be arbitrary, and the 2013 prize already recognised the discovery in the form the statutes allow. I would give the lattice clock the same instrument-led standing without that problem.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators first, arguing that band inversion and spin-orbit coupling predict the effect quantitatively, that it is verified for two decades and that it is arguably overdue, with a Kane, Mele and Molenkamp trio.
responses.response: This is a serious competitor and I rank it among my alternatives. I accept the maturity and the originality, and the theory is strongly confirmed. I disagree with calling the attribution clean. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe effect that Molenkamp measured, and the three-dimensional work of Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore and Balents, and Hasan is also missing, so any trio leaves out people whose contributions were decisive. Zhang is also deceased, which makes the omission impossible to repair. The 2016 topology prize adds the further question of what this adds. I would want the committee to settle that before it settles on this entry.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first and trapped-ion quantum logic second, arguing that these opened new regimes and are mature, with circuit QED complementing the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I would put it differently. Circuit QED is mature and the Blais, Wallraff and Schoelkopf credit is coherent, but the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is so close in subject that I think the committee would be open to the charge of giving the same field two prizes within a few years. The same holds for trapped-ion logic after 2012, where the Cirac and Zoller proposal is the clear originator but Wineland is already a laureate and the experimental slot is contestable among Blatt, Monroe and the NIST group. I would hold these for later years.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 clock-related prizes.
Whether the redefinition of the second will take place soon enough to count as a confirmation of maturity, and whether it should matter to the prize at all.

Whether IceCube (B041) should stay ahead of the clock for people who put a new window on the universe above a metrological advance, given the open question of which individuals to credit within a large collaboration.
My own confidence on condensed-matter attribution for B057 is limited, and I would rely on colleagues for that.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My PhD supervisor David Gross and my frequent co-author Thomas Van Riet work on string theory and cosmology, and none of the shortlisted candidates or credited names is connected to them or to the Uppsala group. I note that Peter Zoller appears in two shortlisted entries (B060 and B006), neither of which is in my preferred configuration.
